summary: Describes the extensions to RSVP-TE signaling required to support Generalized MPLS. GMPLS extends the MPLS control plane beyond packets to time-division, wavelength and spatial switching, as in SONET, SDH and optical networks.

plainLanguage.summary: RSVP-TE is the protocol that sets up reserved label-switched paths in networks. This RFC extends it so it can also set up paths across time slots in SONET or SDH equipment, whole wavelengths of light and whole fibers. It defines the new message formats, how to set up two-way paths, and how to report failures quickly so the right node can repair the path.

questions: how does gmpls set up bidirectional lsps
what is the rsvp notify message
subtitle: How the RSVP-TE signaling protocol was extended to set up paths across time slots, wavelengths and fibers.

tldr.problem: RSVP-TE signaling was built for packet networks, but Generalized MPLS must also set up paths through time-division, wavelength and fiber switches, which need new label formats, two-way paths and faster failure reporting.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3473 adds new RSVP objects such as the Generalized Label Request, Generalized Label, Label Set and Upstream Label, a new Notify message that can reach a non-adjacent node, interface identification for separate control channels, and restart procedures that recover state after a fault.
tldr.outcome: It is the RSVP-TE companion to RFC 3471. It is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, and 14 later RFCs update it.

today: RFC 3473 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the RSVP-TE specification for GMPLS. It has been updated by RFC 4003, RFC 4201, RFC 4420, RFC 4783, RFC 4873, RFC 4874, RFC 4974, RFC 5063, RFC 5151, RFC 5420, RFC 6002, RFC 6003, RFC 6780 and RFC 8359. Read it together with its companion, RFC 3471.

sections.title: Why RSVP-TE Needed GMPLS Extensions
sections.content:
Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) extends MPLS from packet-switching interfaces (PSC) to three more classes: Time-Division Multiplex (TDM), Lambda Switch (LSC) and Fiber-Switch (FSC). The RFC names the examples: SONET/SDH time-division, optical wavelengths (lambdas), and spatial switching from an incoming port or fiber to an outgoing port or fiber.

RFC 3471 gives the generic functional description. RFC 3473 is its companion: it presents the RSVP-TE specific formats and mechanisms needed to support all four classes of interfaces, and its structure parallels RFC 3471. Beyond the generalization itself, it also defines RSVP-TE features for rapid failure notification. The key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY are used as in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP-TE can book a path for packets. GMPLS stretches the same idea to booking whole time slots, wavelengths of light and fibers. This RFC shows how the RSVP-TE messages do that booking.

sections.title: Label Formats and Label Control
sections.content:
The Generalized Label Request object (Class-Num 19, C-Type 4) rides in a Path message. It carries an LSP Encoding Type, a Switching Type and a G-PID. The ingress node sets it, transit nodes pass it on (the Switching Type may be updated hop by hop), and the egress uses it. A node that cannot support the encoding type MUST send a PathErr with a "Routing problem/Unsupported Encoding" indication, and an unsupported Switching Type gets a "Routing problem/Switching Type" indication. The G-PID parameter is normally only examined at the egress. Bandwidth values ride in the SENDER_TSPEC and FLOWSPEC objects, set in the Peak Data Rate field of the Integrated Services objects; other bandwidth parameters are carried transparently and ignored.

The Generalized Label object (Class-Num 16, C-Type 2) travels upstream in Resv messages. A Resv that carries both a generalized and a normal label object is a protocol error. Waveband switching uses C-Type 3 with a Waveband Id, a Start Label and an End Label. When a waveband is switched in a way that mirrors wavelengths about a center frequency, the start and end labels MUST be flipped before the label is forwarded, in both directions for a bidirectional waveband tunnel.

Three tools let an upstream node control what the downstream node picks:

  • Suggested_Label (Class-Number 129) in a Path message hints at a preferred label. Errors in it MUST be ignored, and an ingress node SHOULD NOT transmit data traffic on a suggested label until the downstream node passes a corresponding label upstream.
  • Label_Set (Class-Number 36, C-Type 1) restricts the labels allowed downstream. Its Action field adds or excludes single labels (Actions 0 and 1) or ranges of labels (Actions 2 and 3). A receiving node must pick a label inside the Label Set; if the set becomes empty the request is terminated with a PathErr carrying a "Routing problem/Label Set" indication.
  • Label ERO and RRO subobjects (both Type 3) give explicit label control: up to two label subobjects may follow the IP address or interface of an output link, one for the downstream label and one for the upstream label. The node copies the label into a new Label_Set object or Upstream_Label object on its outgoing Path message, then removes the subobjects from the explicit route.
sections.plainLanguage: A label names the circuit a path uses. These objects let a sender say what kind of circuit it needs, suggest one, restrict the choice to a short list, or name a label outright in the explicit route.

sections.title: Bidirectional LSP Setup
sections.content:
A bidirectional LSP is requested by including an Upstream_Label object (Class-Number 35) in the Path message. The label MUST be valid for forwarding at the time the Path message is sent. A receiver that finds the upstream label unacceptable MUST issue a PathErr with a "Routing problem/Unacceptable label value" indication, and that PathErr MAY include an Acceptable Label Set. An intermediate node must allocate a label on its outgoing interface and establish internal data paths before filling in its own outgoing upstream label and propagating the Path message; if it cannot allocate a label or internal resources it MUST issue a PathErr with a "Routing problem/MPLS label allocation failure" indication.

The terminating node processes the Path message as usual, with one exception: the upstream label can immediately be used to send data traffic back toward the initiator. When a bidirectional LSP is removed, both the upstream and downstream labels are invalidated, and it is no longer valid to send data using them.

Two contention rules apply when both sides set up paths at once. For RSVP contention resolution the node ID is the IP address used in the RSVP_HOP object. When a neighbor's node ID is not yet known, the node should suggest a label chosen at random from the available label space.
sections.plainLanguage: A two-way circuit needs a lane in each direction, so the setup request names the return lane too. If two nodes try to book the same lanes at the same time, rules based on the node's IP address decide who keeps them.

sections.title: Faster Notification of Failures
sections.content:
Ordinary RSVP error messages travel hop by hop, so the node that must restore a failed path hears about the problem only after a string of neighbors relays the news. RFC 3473 adds four notification tools.

  • The Acceptable_Label_Set object (Class-Number 130) can be added to PathErr and ResvErr messages to tell the sender which labels would have been acceptable. Its inclusion is optional, and when included the error message SHOULD carry a "Routing problem/Unacceptable label value" indication.
  • The Notify_Request object (Class-Number 195, with an IPv4 and an IPv6 form) names the node that should be told about a failure. Placed in a Path message it requests upstream notification; placed in a Resv message it requests downstream notification. A transit node SHOULD store the address and include a Notify Request in its outgoing messages. Including the object does not guarantee that a Notify message will be generated.
  • The Notify message (Message Type 21) informs a non-adjacent node of path-related events. It can be sent normally, with other nodes forwarding it toward the target, or encapsulated in a new IP header addressed to the target. It is sent without the router alert option, and a Notify message MUST NOT be generated unless an appropriate Notify Request was received. Notifications to the same node that share the same ERROR_SPEC SHOULD be combined, using a default notification interval of 1 ms, and delivery SHOULD be reliable using the Ack message of RFC 2961.
  • The Path_State_Removed flag (0x04) in the ERROR_SPEC object lets intermediate nodes remove Path state on certain errors. A node that discards the state MAY set the flag; if it is not the session endpoint it SHOULD also generate a PathTear. A node that does not remove the state MUST NOT set the flag.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally, bad news walks from station to station. Here a node can ask to be called directly, so the node responsible for the repair hears about a failure right away and can also learn which labels would have worked.

sections.title: Administrative Status of an LSP
sections.content:
The optional Admin_Status object (Class-Number 196) carries the administrative state of a path in Path and Resv messages. It holds a Reflect (R) bit, a Testing (T) bit, an Administratively down (A) bit and a Delete (D) bit. Absence of the object is the same as receiving one with all values set to zero. Transit nodes update their local state, act on the status per local policy, and propagate the object onward. When an edge node receives the object with the R bit set, it reflects the received values back in the corresponding outgoing message, with the R bit cleared.

The object also drives a graceful delete. Before tearing down a path from the ingress, the ingress sends a Path message with the R and D bits set. After the egress reflects the status in a Resv message with the D bit set, the ingress sends a PathTear and normal RSVP teardown takes place. The egress can start the same procedure by setting R and D in a Resv message.

If the egress does not support the object it will not reflect the status. The ingress SHOULD then wait only a configurable period, 30 seconds by default, before sending PathTear. Intermediate and egress nodes can also ask the ingress to change state by sending a Notify message that carries the Admin_Status object with the D bit set; the R bit MUST NOT be set in such a request, and the sender MUST verify that a Path message with the D bit arrives within the configurable period (30 seconds by default) or else clean up itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node along the path learns whether it is up, in testing, down on purpose, or being deleted. Before closing a path, the sender announces the closure and waits for the far end to confirm, so traffic is not cut off in silence.

sections.title: Separate Control Channels
sections.content:
In some networks the signaling (control) channel is not in-band with the data it controls. The sender of a Path message always chooses the data interface, and on such links it names that interface with a new IF_ID RSVP_HOP object (Class-Num 3, C-Type 3 for IPv4 and C-Type 4 for IPv6). Type-Length-Value (TLV) entries inside the object identify the data channel or channels. For a one-way path a downstream data channel MUST be indicated; for a two-way path a common channel is normally indicated, except on a bundled link where the sender may name a different component link in each direction.

A node receiving TLVs saves their values and returns them in the HOP objects of subsequent Resv messages. The node that originates an IF_ID object MUST keep it consistent with the explicit route; a receiver that finds the two inconsistent MUST send a PathErr with a "Bad Explicit Route object" indication. The object SHOULD NOT be used when no TLVs are needed. The matching IF_ID ERROR_SPEC object (Class-Num 6, C-Type 3 or 4) names the specific interface related to an error in PathErr or ResvErr messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the signaling wires are separate from the wires that carry the data. The Path message then names the exact data interface it wants, in a special field that the next node answers back.

sections.title: Fault Handling and State Recovery
sections.content:
The RFC handles two kinds of control-plane fault. A control channel fault is the loss of signaling communication between two neighbors while both keep running. A nodal fault is a node that loses its control state, for example after a restart, while keeping its data forwarding state. Both rely on the Restart_Cap object (Class-Num 131) carried in RSVP Hello messages, and the object MUST NOT be sent when there is no mechanism to detect data channel failures independent of control channel failures. It holds two 32-bit fields in milliseconds: Restart Time, and Recovery Time, where a Recovery Time of zero means forwarding state was not preserved, and a Restart Time of 0xffffffff means the restart may take an indeterminate interval while the data plane is unaffected.

When a node loses contact with a neighbor that supports recovery, it SHOULD wait at least the neighbor's Restart Time before acting, keep the state of established paths, and send Hello messages with a Dst_Instance value of zero during the wait. It may inform upstream nodes of the loss with a "Control Channel Degraded State" indication, and MUST report restoration with a "Control Channel Active State" indication. The Src_Instance value in the returning Hello message tells the node whether the fault was limited to the control channel or was a nodal fault. In the control-channel case, all shared state SHOULD be refreshed, ideally with Summary Refreshes, within the neighbor's Recovery Time.

After a nodal fault, the restarting node that preserved forwarding state opens a Recovery Period equal to the advertised Recovery Time. A Path message that carries a Recovery_Label object (Class-Number 34) is matched against the preserved forwarding table: if the entry is found, RSVP state is recreated and bound to it. The neighbor of a restarting node refreshes all Path state within about half the advertised Recovery Time, spreading the messages out to avoid overloading the restarted node, and MUST NOT refresh Resv state until the corresponding Path message arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: If a control room goes dark but the tracks keep working, neighbors wait instead of stopping the trains. When the room comes back, they re-confirm which circuit is on which track, using labels the restarted node still remembers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RSVP message security from RFC 2747 provides message integrity and node authentication, and for hop-by-hop messages this document introduces no other new security considerations. The new risk is the Notify message, which can be sent in a non-hop-by-hop fashion and so precludes RSVP's hop-by-hop integrity and authentication model.

Where the same level of security is wanted, standard IPsec in transport mode can be used, with either AH or ESP; the information being communicated is generally not confidential, so encryption need not be used. To permit replay detection, an automated key management system, most likely IKE, SHOULD be used, though configured keys MAY be used. Where IPsec is unavailable and security is required, Notify messages MUST be sent hop by hop, or the sending of non-hop-by-hop Notify messages can be disabled.
sections.plainLanguage: A Notify message can skip the stations next door, so the usual neighbor-to-neighbor checks do not cover it. Either protect the message with IPsec, or force it to travel station to station.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length of the object in bytes.

fields.name: LSP Enc. Type
fields.desc: Encoding of the path being requested, set by the ingress.

fields.name: Switching Type
fields.desc: Type of switching requested on a link; may be updated hop by hop.

fields.name: G-PID
fields.desc: Identifier of the payload carried by the path, normally checked at the egress.

items.desc: No label could be chosen from the Label Set, or the object could not be parsed.

items.desc: The Switching Type is not supported on the incoming interface.

items.desc: The LSP Encoding Type cannot be supported.

items.desc: The requested protection cannot be satisfied.

items.desc: Control communication with a neighbor has been restored.

items.label: Notify Error / Control Channel Degraded State
items.desc: Control communication with a neighbor has been lost.
